alt: A tree diagram: the thesis is the trunk, each paragraph’s claim is a branch and the evidence is the leaves. A note adds that some theses preview the structure of the argument and others do not.
caption: Find the thesis, then describe what it shows about the argument’s structure.

after: ## A thesis is not always one sentence, and not always stated
alt: Four page schematics with the thesis highlighted: at the start (thesis first), at the end (thesis last), across the end of one paragraph and the start of the next (across sentences), and nowhere stated but carried by the whole text (implied).
caption: The thesis may come first, last, across sentences, or only by implication.

after: ## Thesis versus things that are not the thesis
alt: The thesis sits in the centre, defined as the sentence every paragraph together tries to prove. Around it are six look-alikes with examples: a topic, a fact, a sub-claim, an announcement, a counterargument and a question.
caption: A thesis is what every paragraph, taken together, is trying to prove.

after: ## A public-domain example of a stated thesis: the Declaration of Sentiments (1848)
alt: The Declaration of Independence’s “all men are created equal” is set above the Declaration of Sentiments’ “all men and women are created equal”, with “and women” highlighted. Below, the stated thesis is supported by the grievances and resolutions that follow.
caption: Two added words, “and women”, carry the whole argument.

after: ## A public-domain example of an implied thesis: Swift's "A Modest Proposal" (1729)
alt: Two boxes face each other: the narrator calmly proposes that the poor of Ireland sell their children as food; Swift implies that the poor are already treated as a commodity and real reform is needed. Below, context, the satirical target and the rejected remedies reveal the implied thesis.
caption: In satire, the writer’s thesis can be the opposite of the narrator’s proposal.

after: ## Worked example 1: a delayed thesis (written by Marlbridge)
alt: The three paragraphs of the Orchard Road passage as a downward flow. Paragraph one sets out the loss, including a fact; paragraph two gives the counterargument and a sub-claim; paragraph three states the thesis that the council should count what trees give as carefully as what they cost.
caption: Summarise each paragraph, then find the claim they all support.
